outline.chapter_title: Motivation and Overview: Why Stable RL for LLMs Needs GSPO
outline.description: Introduce the role of reinforcement learning in scaling large language models and the central challenge of maintaining stability at scale. Summarize the limitations of GRPO observed in practice (instability, collapse) and present GSPO as a principled, sequence-level alternative. Provide a high-level roadmap of the textbook and the paper’s main contributions.
subtopics: RL as a driver of advanced capabilities in LLMs (math, code, long-form reasoning)
Stability as the prerequisite for scaling RL compute
Empirical instability and collapse with GRPO for large/long outputs
GSPO’s core idea: sequence-level importance weighting and clipping
Contributions: stability, efficiency, MoE robustness, infrastructure simplification

outline.description: Lay down the formal setup used throughout: policies as autoregressive LMs, queries and responses, and verifier-provided rewards. Clarify how batches, groups, and off-policy updates arise in practical training pipelines.
subtopics: Policy as an autoregressive language model
Queries, responses, and sequence likelihoods
Verifier and bounded reward in [0, 1]
Query set and sampling procedures
Large-batch rollouts, mini-batch gradient updates, and off-policy effects
Why clipping is necessary in off-policy training

outline.description: Review PPO as a widely used on-policy algorithm with token-level importance ratios and value-based advantage estimation. Explain GRPO’s value-free design using group-normalized rewards and token-level clipping, along with its practical appeal and emerging limitations.
subtopics: PPO objective with token-level importance ratios and clipping
Role and burden of the value model in PPO
GRPO objective: group-based (value-free) advantage estimation
Token-level ratios under GRPO and shared token advantages
Practical benefits of GRPO and early successes
Limitations: reliance on token-level correction and observed instability

outline.chapter_title: Diagnosing GRPO Instability: Importance Sampling and the Unit-of-Reward Principle
outline.description: Develop the theoretical motivation for GSPO by analyzing how importance sampling should be used and why GRPO’s token-level weighting is ill-posed. Emphasize the mismatch between token-level optimization and sequence-level rewards, and how this leads to high-variance gradients and collapse.
subtopics: Importance sampling basics: correcting distribution mismatch via weights
Why multiple samples are needed for stable importance-weighted estimates
GRPO’s single-sample token-level weights and variance inflation
Accumulation of noise over long sequences
Clipping interactions that exacerbate instability
Unit-of-optimization should match unit-of-reward (sequence-level)

outline.chapter_title: The GSPO Algorithm: Sequence-Level Clipping and Optimization
outline.description: Present GSPO’s core objective with sequence-level importance ratios and group-normalized advantages. Explain length normalization, response-level clipping, and how GSPO restores principled off-policy correction aligned with sequence-level rewards.
subtopics: Sequence-level importance ratio based on response likelihood
Length normalization: exponent 1/|y| to control variance and scale
Group-based z-score advantage (mean/std over responses per query)
Sequence-level clipping of entire responses
Alignment of reward unit and optimization unit
Magnitude differences in clipping ranges versus GRPO and why they arise

outline.chapter_title: Gradient Analysis and Comparison to GRPO
outline.description: Derive GSPO’s gradient and contrast it with GRPO’s token-weighted gradient. Show how GSPO’s equal weighting of tokens within a response improves stability and reduces variance, especially for long generations.
subtopics: GSPO gradient: response-level weight times sum of token log-likelihood gradients
GRPO gradient: per-token importance weights multiply token gradients
Consequences of unequal token weights when advantages are positive or negative
Variance accumulation in GRPO vs. uniform within-response weighting in GSPO
Why GSPO mitigates unpredictable dynamics over training

outline.chapter_title: GSPO-token: Per-Token Advantage with Sequence-Level Reweighting
outline.description: Introduce GSPO-token for scenarios needing token-wise credits (e.g., multi-turn RL). Explain the stop-gradient construction that preserves sequence-level reweighting while allowing token-specific advantages, and show equivalence to GSPO when token advantages match.
subtopics: Motivation: finer-grained credit assignment across tokens or turns
Definition of per-token s_{i,t} with stop-gradient (detach)
Numerical equality of s_{i,t} and s_i and implications
Gradient derivation and interpretation
Equivalence to GSPO when all token advantages are identical
When to prefer GSPO-token in practice

outline.chapter_title: Practical Training with GSPO: Implementation and Tuning
outline.description: Translate the algorithm into a robust training recipe. Cover batching, computing sequence likelihoods efficiently, setting clipping thresholds, reward normalization, optional KL regularization, and monitoring. Highlight how GSPO eases inference–training engine mismatches.
subtopics: Constructing groups: G responses per query and batch organization
Mini-batch updates and off-policy considerations
Efficient computation of sequence likelihoods and normalized ratios
Choosing clipping ranges (different scale than token-level methods)
Reward normalization details (mean/std; stability floors for std)
Optional KL regularization and scheduling
Generation length schedules and query set refresh strategies
Monitoring: response-level clipping fraction, s_i histograms, reward stats
Handling precision discrepancies: using inference-engine likelihoods directly
Compute and memory tips for large models and long outputs

outline.chapter_title: GSPO for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): Stability Without Routing Replay
outline.description: Explain MoE-specific instability under GRPO due to expert-activation volatility and the previously required Routing Replay workaround. Show why GSPO’s sequence-level focus eliminates this need, simplifying infrastructure and enabling full MoE capacity.
subtopics: MoE routing and expert-activation volatility across updates
Why GRPO’s token-level ratios become unstable in MoE training
Routing Replay: stabilizing GRPO via cached routing (costs and limits)
GSPO’s robustness: stability of sequence likelihood vs. token likelihoods
Removal of Routing Replay and infrastructure simplification
Practical benefits for deep and large MoE models

outline.description: Detail the experimental setup and summarize the key findings. Emphasize GSPO’s stable training, superior efficiency vs. GRPO, better benchmark results, and the counterintuitive but revealing clipping-fraction observation.
subtopics: Setup: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base cold start; rollout batches split into 4 mini-batches
GSPO vs. GRPO hyperparameters (distinct clipping ranges)
Benchmarks: AIME’24 (Pass@1 over 32), LiveCodeBench 202410–202502 (Pass@1 over 8), Codeforces (Elo)
Results: continuous improvements with more compute, query updates, and longer generations
Training efficiency gains relative to GRPO under equal compute
Clipping fractions: GSPO clips far more tokens yet learns faster
Role of GSPO in Qwen3 performance improvements

outline.description: Discuss scope and assumptions, highlight potential extensions, and distill actionable lessons. Conclude with a concise synthesis of why GSPO forms a stable, scalable foundation for RL with LLMs.
subtopics: Dependence on reward quality and group-normalization stability
Tuning length normalization and alternative sequence-level reweightings
Interplay with KL regularization and other constraints
Applying GSPO to multi-turn RL, partial rollouts, and diverse modalities
Open questions: theory of sequence-level IS variance, credit assignment
Key takeaways and practical checklist for adopting GSPO
